text.kicker: INTERNAL · THE STORY ARC IN PROSE · NOT FOR THE CUT
text.title: One argument in five chapters
text.subtitle: The trader who loses money is not short of rules. He is short of an operator.
text.body:
Ken opens on the two pathologies he says he lives with every day, revenge and rigidity, and on the gate at the post on the way to work, where the same chimp shows up that shows up in a trade (chapter 1, s01 and s03). Chapter 1b asks the question the course is named for: how long are you going to watch the monkey drive? His answer is not willpower. It is a caretaker function that is instantly activated, and an internal team, from the designer of the trade to the scout, so that the operator has one job: make the decision (s05, s06).

Chapter 2 gives the trade a shape he can run under pressure, the four questions from the soccer field: can we protect our goal, can we get the ball, can I go to the goal, can I shoot and score, with the coach managing the emotional states between plays (s08, s09). Chapter 3 turns the lens on the operator: Aristotle's spectrum from timidity to pride, cynicism as costly as pride, the parable of the talents, then the A/B/C bands and the mark you make at the close, rating the session rather than the P&L (s11 to s17).

Chapter 4 rations the firepower: three machine guns taking turns, parsimonious rules, cutting away the Frankenstein creature to the minimum mission-essential set, respecting the few indicators you keep (s19 to s23). Chapter 5 puts a number on the whole book: portfolio heat defined as the sum of open risk, sizing against the goal rather than against the gut, and the dynamic threshold (s25 to s27). The arc runs self, then trade, then capital, and ends on his own words: let's go, buckle up.

text.title: The part of trading no indicator covers
text.subtitle: About forty minutes with Dr. Ken Long on the person at the controls.
text.body:
Ken names the two habits he says he lives with every day, revenge and rigidity, and shows where they turn up: on the drive to work, and in the next trade after a loss. He asks how long you are going to watch the monkey drive, and answers with a caretaker function and an internal team that leaves the operator one job: make the decision.

He gives every trade four questions borrowed from the soccer field. Can we protect our goal? Can we get the ball? Can I go to the goal? Can I shoot and score? He grades the trader instead of the P&L, with Aristotle's spectrum from timidity to pride and the A, B and C bands you mark at the close of every session.

He rations the work with three machine guns and the minimum mission-essential set, and he puts a number on the whole book: portfolio heat, sizing against the goal, and the dynamic threshold that caps the stack.

Five chapters cut from four of his live sessions, in his own words, with new animation drawn to what he says.

segments.label: EXPLAINER + cut tail: the dynamic threshold ('Let's go. Buckle up.' RESTORED)
segments.vo_script: Portfolio heat is the sum of the open risk across every position you hold, as a share of your risk capital. A dynamic risk threshold moves that ceiling with results. After a run of losses it tightens; after wins it loosens back toward the plan. The gut sets the size of each rung. The threshold caps the stack. When the stack reaches the line, no new position goes on until one comes off. Here is Ken on laying the numbers out to your gut.
